Cluster Sequences by Dissimilarity

Source: R/cluster_data.R
build_clusters.Rd

build_clusters() splits a set of sequences into k groups of similar sequences. It computes the dissimilarity between every pair of sequences (the Hamming distance, an edit distance, a q-gram distance or the Jaro-Winkler distance) and partitions that matrix with PAM (partitioning around medoids) or a hierarchical method. It takes wide sequence data, a netobject or bare cograph_network built from sequences, or a tna model. A one-hot network built with "relative", "frequency" or "co_occurrence" is clustered by unit, each actor's or session's windows forming one sequence; a wtna network is refused (see data). Covariates can be related to the clusters after the fit (see covariates); they never change the assignments.

Every dissimilarity and method returns k groups, whether or not the sequences fall into groups. The average silhouette width (Rousseeuw, 1987), which print() reports, compares each sequence's mean dissimilarity to its own cluster with that to the nearest other cluster: it runs from -1 to 1, values near 1 meaning well-separated clusters and values near 0 overlapping ones. It describes one solution and is not a test. Compare values of k, dissimilarities and methods with cluster_choice(), check the classification with cluster_diagnostics(), and build one network per cluster with build_network() (or cluster_network() in one call) to see how the groups differ.

Usage

build_clusters(
  data,
  k,
  dissimilarity = "hamming",
  method = "pam",
  na_syms = c("*", "%"),
  weighted = FALSE,
  lambda = 1,
  seed = NULL,
  q = 2L,
  p = 0.1,
  covariates = NULL,
  estimator = c("auto", "firth", "multinom", "chisq"),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'net_clustering'
print(x, digits = 3L, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_clustering'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_clustering'
plot(
  x,
  type = c("silhouette", "mds", "heatmap", "predictors"),
  combined = TRUE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'tidy_covariates'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

The sequences: a data frame or matrix with one row per sequence and one column per position, holding state names; a netobject or bare cograph_network built from sequences with method "relative", "frequency", "co_occurrence" or "attention", whose stored sequences are used; or a tna model, whose integer-coded sequences are decoded to their labels. Columns of a data frame take the same roles as in build_network(): an id or a covariate is not a position, and the columns set aside are named in a message and kept as metadata. A one-hot network needs an actor or session to define its units. A one-hot network without one, and a network of any other method, raise an error of class nestimate_bad_input.

k

The number of clusters, a whole number from 2 to one less than the number of sequences. Required.

dissimilarity

How two sequences are compared. "hamming" (default) counts the positions where they differ. "lv" (Levenshtein) counts the insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one into the other; "osa" (optimal string alignment) and "dl" (Damerau-Levenshtein) also count a swap of two adjacent states as one edit; "lcs" counts the states left unpaired by their longest common subsequence. "qgram", "cosine" and "jaccard" compare the runs of q consecutive states (q-grams) the sequences contain: the summed absolute difference of their counts, one minus the cosine similarity of the counts, and one minus the share of distinct q-grams they have in common. "jw" is the Jaro-Winkler distance, which weighs agreement in the first states more (see p).

method

The clustering algorithm. "pam" (default) partitions around medoids: it chooses k sequences as centres and assigns every sequence to the nearest one (Kaufman & Rousseeuw, 1990). "ward.D2", "ward.D", "complete", "average", "single", "mcquitty", "median" and "centroid" build a tree with stats::hclust() using that linkage and cut it into k groups.

na_syms

The symbols read as missing values, besides NA. Default c("*", "%"). A missing cell is not dropped from a comparison: it is treated as one more state, so two missing cells at the same position match and a missing cell against an observed state is a mismatch (a distance of 1 for Hamming). This is the usual rule for aligned sequences, because dropping missing cells pair by pair would change each pair's effective length and break the metric. For every dissimilarity except Hamming, a sequence ends at its last observed state, so trailing missing cells are not compared. To treat missing cells differently, drop or recode them before the call.

weighted

Whether to weight the Hamming distance by position, so that a difference early in the sequences counts more than a late one (see lambda). Default FALSE. With any dissimilarity other than "hamming", TRUE raises an error.

lambda

The decay rate of the position weights when weighted = TRUE: position \(t\) gets weight \(e^{-\lambda (t - 1)}\), so a larger value puts more of the distance on the earlier positions. A finite non-negative number; default 1. Ignored, and stored as 0, when weighted = FALSE.

seed

An integer used as the random seed for clustering; the session's own random stream is left as it was. Default NULL. PAM and the hierarchical methods are deterministic, so it does not change the clusters; it is stored with the result.

q

The length of the q-grams compared by "qgram", "cosine" and "jaccard", a positive whole number. Default 2. Ignored by the other dissimilarities.

p

The Winkler prefix weight of "jw": how much agreement in the first states (up to four) lowers the Jaro distance, from 0 (the plain Jaro distance) to 0.25. Default 0.1. Ignored by the other dissimilarities.

covariates

Variables describing each sequence (such as an achievement level or a course), related to the clusters after they are found; they never change the assignments. Give a column name, a character vector of names, a one-sided formula such as ~ Age + Gender (or the string "Age + Gender"), or a data frame with one row per sequence, all of whose columns are used. For a netobject or cograph_network, names are looked up in its metadata first and then among the columns of its data, so a typical call is build_clusters(net, k = 3, covariates = "Achiever"); for a data frame or matrix, among its columns. A tna model takes only the data-frame form. Named covariate columns are taken out of the sequence data before the distances are computed, and so are the columns of a supplied data frame that match a sequence column in name and values; a sequence column that shares only a name is kept. For a network, a name found in its metadata leaves a same-named data column in place as a sequence position. Rows with a missing covariate are left out of the analysis with a warning, and a constant covariate raises an error. How the analysis is run is set by estimator. Default NULL (none).

estimator

How the relation between the covariates and the clusters is estimated; it never affects the clustering. "auto" (default) fits a multinomial logit of cluster membership on the covariates: with Firth's bias-reduced penalised likelihood (brglm2::brmultinom(), finite under quasi-complete separation) when a cell of the cluster-by-covariate table of a categorical covariate holds fewer than 5 sequences, and with nnet::multinom() otherwise. "firth" forces the Firth fit, which is about 200 times slower on well-conditioned data. "multinom" forces classical maximum likelihood and warns that rare cells can give extreme odds ratios with degenerate confidence intervals. "chisq" runs descriptive tests instead of a logit, as WeightedCluster does: for each categorical covariate a chi-square test with Cramer's V and standardised adjusted residuals, for each numeric one a Kruskal-Wallis test with eta-squared. Ignored without covariates.

...

Not used: an extra argument raises an error, here and in the print(), summary() and plot() methods for a net_clustering. print() of a tidy_covariates table ignores it.

x

For the print() and plot() methods: a net_clustering; for print(), also the tidy_covariates table that summary() returns.

digits

For print() of a net_clustering: decimal places of the silhouette width and the within-cluster distances, a non-negative whole number. Default 3.

object

For summary(): a net_clustering.

type

For plot(): the view. "silhouette" (default) draws each sequence's silhouette width as a bar, grouped by cluster, with the average as a dashed line; "mds" places the sequences on the first two dimensions of a classical multidimensional scaling of the distances, coloured by cluster; "heatmap" draws the distance matrix with the sequences ordered by cluster; "predictors" draws a forest plot of the covariates' odds ratios (log scale) for each cluster against the reference cluster. "predictors" needs a fit with covariates and a logit estimator; with estimator = "chisq", which has no odds ratios, it raises an error.

combined

For plot() with type = "predictors": TRUE (default) draws one plot with a panel per non-reference cluster; FALSE returns a list of plots, one per non-reference cluster. Ignored by the other views.

Value

A net_clustering object. print() shows the method, dissimilarity and average silhouette width, then one row per cluster with its size (count and percentage), mean within-cluster distance and, for PAM, its medoid; after a logit covariate analysis it adds a line naming the predictors. summary() prints the method, dissimilarity and average silhouette width and a per-cluster table of sizes and mean within-cluster distances, followed by the covariate analysis when there is one, and returns a per-cluster table, or the covariate table after a covariate analysis (see the methods' return value below). plot() draws the silhouette widths, a map of the distances, the distance matrix or the covariate effects. build_network() turns the clustering into one network per cluster (a netobject_group), and cluster_diagnostics() and session_ids() give the classification quality and each sequence's cluster. The object's fields:

data

The sequence positions that were clustered, one row per sequence: covariates and set-aside columns are removed, and a one-hot network gives one row per unit.

k

Number of clusters.

assignments

Integer vector of cluster memberships (1 to k), one per sequence in row order.

silhouette

Average silhouette width over all sequences.

sizes

Named integer vector of cluster sizes.

method

Clustering method used.

dissimilarity

Dissimilarity used.

distance

The pairwise dissimilarities, a dist object.

medoids

For PAM, the row numbers of the k medoid sequences; NULL for the hierarchical methods.

seed

Seed given (or NULL).

weighted

Whether weighted Hamming was used.

lambda

Decay rate used (0 when not weighted).

covariates

The covariate analysis (a list; see estimator), or NULL when covariates = NULL.

network_method, build_args

For netobject input, the source network's method and stored build arguments, so per-cluster networks can be rebuilt the same way. NULL otherwise, and build_args is NULL for a one-hot network.

metadata

For netobject input, its per-sequence metadata, one row per clustered sequence, so session_ids can name each sequence. For a data frame, the columns set aside as covariates (see data). NULL otherwise, and for a one-hot network.

htna_partition

For HTNA input, the preserved node-to-actor partition used to restore HTNA children when networks are built.

For the print() methods: the input, invisibly. print() of a tidy_covariates table prints a header naming the estimator, then the table. For summary(): a data frame with one row per cluster and columns cluster, size and mean_within_dist, returned visibly after the printed summary. For a clustering fitted with covariates, the printed summary adds the covariate profiles and the logit or test tables, and a tidy_covariates data frame is returned invisibly instead: one row per cluster and predictor (cluster, predictor, OR, CI_low, CI_high, p, sig) for a logit, or one row per covariate (variable, type, statistic, df, p, effect, effect_kind, sig) for estimator = "chisq", with the per-cluster table, fit statistics and profiles attached as attributes. For plot(): a ggplot object, drawn and returned invisibly; with type = "predictors" and combined = FALSE, a list of ggplot objects, one per non-reference cluster and named by it, returned invisibly without drawing.

Details

With the stringdist package installed, the distances are computed by stringdist::stringdistmatrix() in C, many times faster than the base R implementation for the edit distances. The base R implementation is used when stringdist is absent, for weighted Hamming, and when the data hold 62 or more states.

References

Kaufman, L., & Rousseeuw, P. J. (1990). Finding Groups in Data: An Introduction to Cluster Analysis. Wiley.

Rousseeuw, P. J. (1987). Silhouettes: A graphical aid to the interpretation and validation of cluster analysis. Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics, 20, 53–65. doi:10.1016/0377-0427(87)90125-7

Examples

seqs <- data.frame(V1 = c("A","B","C","A","B"), V2 = c("B","C","A","B","A"),
                   V3 = c("C","A","B","C","B"))
cl <- build_clusters(seqs, k = 2)
cl
#> Sequence Clustering [pam]
#>   Sequences: 5  |  Clusters: 2
#>   Dissimilarity: hamming
#>   Quality: silhouette = 0.600
#> 
#>   Cluster  N          Mean within-dist  Medoid
#>   1        2 (40.0%)  0.000             4
#>   2        3 (60.0%)  2.000             5
# \donttest{
seqs <- data.frame(
  V1 = sample(LETTERS[1:3], 20, TRUE), V2 = sample(LETTERS[1:3], 20, TRUE),
  V3 = sample(LETTERS[1:3], 20, TRUE), V4 = sample(LETTERS[1:3], 20, TRUE)
)
cl <- build_clusters(seqs, k = 2)
print(cl)
#> Sequence Clustering [pam]
#>   Sequences: 20  |  Clusters: 2
#>   Dissimilarity: hamming
#>   Quality: silhouette = 0.315
#> 
#>   Cluster  N           Mean within-dist  Medoid
#>   1        9 (45.0%)   2.333             5
#>   2        11 (55.0%)  2.000             15
summary(cl)
#> Sequence Clustering Summary
#>   Method:        pam 
#>   Dissimilarity: hamming 
#>   Silhouette:    0.315 
#> 
#> Per-cluster statistics:
#>  cluster size mean_within_dist
#>        1    9         2.333333
#>        2   11         2.000000
#>   cluster size mean_within_dist
#> 1       1    9         2.333333
#> 2       2   11         2.000000
# }
